title: Greedy Best-First in Lisbon: Fast… or Wrong? ⚡
description: Watch Greedy Best-First Search rush toward the goal using only a heuristic—then see where it can fail on real map-like graphs. Compare the resulting path shape to what A* would do on the same neighborhood layout.
ig_caption:
Greedy Best-First Search vs A*: Pathfinding Comparison — why does Greedy sprint to the goal ⚡ (and when does it betray you)?

In this Lisbon (Alfama) grid simulation, Greedy Best-First uses just the heuristic h(n) (usually straight-line distance) to pick the “most promising” next node.
- Priority = lowest h(n)
- It does NOT balance “cost so far + estimate” like A*

What you’ll notice:
1) Greedy often finds a path quickly… because it keeps choosing nodes that look closest to the destination.
2) But if the heuristic is misleading (detours that *look* farther), it can get trapped in a locally “best-looking” route.
3) A* adds g(n) (actual cost so far) + h(n), making it far more robust in tricky obstacle layouts.

Takeaway: Greedy Best-First is fast when your heuristic is trustworthy; A* is safer when paths have hidden costs.

Debate question: Would you rather optimize for speed (Greedy) or reliability (A*) when building real routing in AI games/robots?
